x: In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Commentary on Sūrat al-Qiyāmah.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “No indeed! I swear by the Day of Resurrection, and I swear by the self-reproaching soul. Does the human being think We will never gather his bones? Yes indeed, We are able even to restore his fingertips” (75:1–4). Abū Jaʿfar said the reciters differed in reading “lā uqsimu bi-yawm al-qiyāmah.” Most regional reciters read “lā” separately from “uqsimu,” while al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿraj reportedly read la-uqsimu, joining the lām to the verb as an emphatic oath: “I swear by the Day of Resurrection.” The only reading I consider permissible here is “lā” separate and “uqsimu” beginning a new phrase, as the regional reciters read it, since the authoritative reciters agree upon it. Those who read it this way differed in interpretation.
Some said “lā” is extra, so the meaning is simply “I swear by the Day of Resurrection.”
Those who said this include: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said “I swear by the Day of Resurrection.” Another report from him gives the same.

Others said “lā” entered to reinforce the statement. Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh said “lā” in “No indeed! I swear” emphasizes the oath, as in saying, “No, by God!” Some Kufan grammarians said “lā” rejects something previously said by the polytheists, who denied Paradise and Hell, after which the oath begins: “I swear by the Day of Resurrection.” They said that an oath preceded by a rejection must have “lā” before it, to distinguish an oath that rejects a claim from a newly initiated oath. They noted the difference between beginning “By God, the Messenger is truly in the right” and saying “No, by God, the Messenger is truly in the right,” which rejects those who deny him.

evidence.text: Abū Jaʿfar said the reciters differed in reading “lā uqsimu bi-yawm al-qiyāmah.”

Most regional reciters read “lā” separately from “uqsimu,” while al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿraj reportedly read la-uqsimu, joining the lām to the verb as an emphatic oath: “I swear by the Day of Resurrection.”
The only reading I consider permissible here is “lā” separate and “uqsimu” beginning a new phrase, as the regional reciters read it, since the authoritative reciters agree upon it.
Those who read it this way differed in interpretation.

x: They also differed over whether the verse is an oath.

Some said it is: our Lord swore by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul. Ibn ʿAbbās told Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, when asked about “No indeed! I swear by the Day of Resurrection”: “Your Lord swears by whatever He wills of His creation.” Qatādah said He swore by both.

Others said He swore by the Day of Resurrection but did not swear by the self-reproaching soul; they interpreted “And I do not swear by the self-reproaching soul” as “I do not swear by it.” Al-Ḥasan said He swore by the Day of Resurrection, but did not swear by the self-reproaching soul. In my view, the soundest interpretation is that God swore by both the Day of Resurrection and the self-reproaching soul, and that “lā” rejects a preceding statement made by some people, then answers them. This is preferable because in ordinary conversation, when someone says, “No, by God, I will not do this,” “no” rejects what came before, while “by God” begins the oath. The same applies to “No, I swear by God.” Other similar expressions should be understood this way unless evidence requires another meaning. Moreover, all authorities agree that “I swear by the Day of Resurrection” is an oath; the same applies to “I swear by the self-reproaching soul,” unless evidence shows one is an oath and the other a statement.

We have shown that joining the lām in “la-uqsimu” is impermissible because it conflicts with the reading agreed upon by the authoritative reciters. The meaning is therefore: No—the matter is not as you claim, people, that God will not raise His servants alive after death. I swear by the Day of Resurrection.
Some people used to say that each person’s resurrection is their death.

Among those who said this: al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah related that people say “the Resurrection, the Resurrection,” but each person’s resurrection is their death. Abū Qays said at a funeral where ʿAlqamah was present, after the burial: “For this person, his Resurrection has come.” Regarding “And I swear by the self-reproaching soul”: the interpreters differed.

Some said it means the soul that reproaches itself for good and evil. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said it reproaches itself for good and evil. ʿIkrimah gave the same explanation. Ibn ʿAbbās described it as a blameworthy soul.

evidence.text: We have shown that joining the lām in “la-uqsimu” is impermissible because it conflicts with the reading agreed upon by the authoritative reciters.

x: Others said it means a soul that reproaches itself and regrets what it missed. Mujāhid said it regrets what passed and blames itself for it.
Others said it means the wicked soul. Qatādah said it means the sinful soul.

Others said it means the blameworthy soul. Ibn ʿAbbās said: “The blameworthy one.” Though the words of those who offered these interpretations differ, their meanings are close. The interpretation most consistent with the verse’s apparent meaning is that the soul reproaches itself for good and evil and regrets what it missed. All reciters agree that “lā” is separate from “uqsimu.” Regarding “Does the human being think We will never gather his bones?” God Most High says: Does the son of Adam think We cannot gather his bones after they have disintegrated? Indeed, We are able to do even more: restore his fingertips—his fingers and toes—so that they could be made into a single hoof like a camel’s or a donkey’s. Then he would take food only with his mouth, like other animals. Instead, God separated his fingers so he can grasp, reach, close and open his hand as he wishes, perfecting his creation.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās said: If God wished, He could make the hand a hoof or a fetlock. He also said God could make the palm solid like a camel’s foot. Another report from him gives the same explanation. ʿIkrimah explained it as making the hand like a camel’s hoof or a donkey’s fetlock. Al-Ḥasan said: God made the hand with fingers that one can close and open; had He wished, He could have joined them together, leaving you to scrape the earth with your mouth. Instead, He formed you beautifully. Abū Rajāʾ said ʿIkrimah was asked and replied that God could have made the hand like a camel’s hoof. Mujāhid explained “restore his fingertips” as restoring his feet like a camel’s hoof, leaving him unable to do anything with them. Qatādah said: By God, our Lord is able to make his fingertips like an animal’s hoof or a camel’s foot. Had He wished, He would have done so, and the person would pick up food with his mouth.

evidence.text: All reciters agree that “lā” is separate from “uqsimu.”

x: Ibn ʿAbbās said: “Indeed, We are able to restore his fingertips”—I am able to make his hand a solid mass, like the hoof of a camel. Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says God can make the hand like a camel’s hoof or a donkey’s fetlock. ʿIkrimah said the same. Al-Ḥasan said that God made the hand with fingers one can close and open; had He wished, He could have joined them, leaving a person to scrape the ground with his mouth. Instead, He formed him beautifully. Abū Rajāʾ said ʿIkrimah was asked and replied that God could have made it like a camel’s hoof. Mujāhid said “restore his fingertips” means restore his feet like a camel’s hoof, so he could do nothing with them. Qatādah said: By God, our Lord is able to make his fingertips like an animal’s hoof or a camel’s foot. Had He wished, He would have done so, and he would pick up food with his mouth. Qatādah said God could have made his fingertips like a camel’s hoof or an animal’s fetlock.
Al-Ḍaḥḥāk explained “fingertips” as fingers and said God is able to make them like a camel’s hoof. Arabic grammarians differed over why “qādirīn” is in the accusative.

Some said it stands in place of “We do,” and is therefore accusative when changed into an active participle. The meaning would be: Does the human think We cannot gather his bones? Indeed, We are able to restore his fingertips. Some Kufan grammarians said it is separated from “We gather,” as if the meaning were: Does he think We are unable to do so? Indeed, We are able—more powerful than you. They rejected the explanation that the accusative comes merely from changing “We are able” into an active participle: a verb does not become accusative simply by changing “he does” to “doing.” You can say “Are you coming to us?” and change it to “Are you coming?” but it would be wrong to say “coming” in the accusative. They cited al-Farazdaq’s verse: “I have sworn that I will never insult a Muslim, nor will false speech leave my mouth.” They said the poet meant “I will not insult” and “it will not leave,” changing the latter to “leaving” in the accusative.

But it is accusative because he meant “I have pledged to my Lord that I will insult no one and no false speech will leave my mouth.” Some Basran grammarians said the accusative is linked to “We gather”: We will gather them, able to restore his fingertips. This latter analysis better accords with Arabic grammar.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “Rather, the human being wants to persist in sin ahead of him. He asks, ‘When is the Day of Resurrection?’ When the sight is dazzled, the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are brought together, that day the human being will say, ‘Where can I flee?’ No indeed! There is no refuge. To your Lord that day is the final destination” (75:5–12).

The son of Adam does not fail to understand that his Lord can gather his bones; rather, he wants to keep going forward in disobeying God, without anything turning him away or his ever repenting. He keeps putting off repentance.

Those who said this include: Ibn ʿAbbās explained “the human being wants to persist in sin ahead of him” as continuing forward. Another report says it refers to wishful thinking: a person says, “I will act, then repent before the Day of Resurrection”; it is also said to mean denying the truth before the Resurrection. Mujāhid said it means continuing on ahead, headlong. Al-Ḥasan said the son of Adam’s soul keeps drawing him step by step toward disobedience, except for those God protects. Another report from al-Ḥasan says it means continuing in sin. Al-Suddī said it means continuing forward. ʿIkrimah said it means continuing forward without ceasing from sin. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the person says, “I will repent later.”

Others said it means that a person persistently pursues worldly life and does not remember death. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it is wishful thinking: a person hopes to live and gain this and that from the world, but does not remember death.

Others said it means the disbelieving human wants to deny the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means the disbeliever denies the reckoning. Ibn Zayd said he denies what lies ahead—the Day of Resurrection and the reckoning.
Others said it means the human wishes to deny the truth before the Resurrection; on this interpretation, “ahead of him” refers to the Resurrection. We have already cited reports for this view.

Regarding “He asks, ‘When is the Day of Resurrection?’”: God Most High says that the son of Adam, who keeps persisting in disobedience, asks, “When will the Day of Resurrection be?” He does so to delay repentance. God clarifies it for him: “When the sight is dazzled, the moon is eclipsed, and the sun and moon are brought together,” to the end of the passage.

The interpreters said similarly. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: He says, “I will repent later,” so God clarifies it for him with “When the sight is dazzled…” Qatādah said he asks, “When is the Day of Resurrection?” ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, said: Whoever asks about the Day of Resurrection should recite this surah. Ibn Zayd asked when it would happen, then recited “and the sun and moon are brought together,” saying this is how the Day of Resurrection will occur.

evidence.text: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, said: Whoever asks about the Day of Resurrection should recite this surah.

x: Regarding “When the sight is dazzled”: the reciters differed. Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read baraqa with fatḥah on the rāʾ, meaning the eye is fixed and wide open at death. Shaybah, Abū ʿAmr, and most Kufan reciters read bariqa with kasrah, meaning it is terrified and stunned. Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf related that he asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, who said the kasrah reading means “confused.” ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq said the fatḥah is used of a dried colocynth: “The colocynth shines, but how does the eye shine?” Abū ʿAmr replied: “The colocynth, fire, and lightning shine, but the eye is fixed at death.” Abū Isḥāq said he learned his reading from the elders, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim and his associates. Abū ʿAmr replied that he did not take his reading from Naṣr and his associates, but seemed to mean he took it from the people of the Ḥijāz. In our view the reading with kasrah, “bariqa,” is preferable: the eye is terrified, stunned, and opened wide by the horror of the Day of Resurrection and the terror of death.

Arabic poetry supports this meaning. A narrator recited to me a line by a man of Kilāb: “When Ibn Ṣubayḥ came to me seeking help, I gave him a pale she-camel, and he was stunned.” Abū Zakariyyā al-Farrāʾ related another verse: “Ḥanānah mourned a Ṭūbālah, grazing on dry ʿishriq. Mourn for yourself, do not mourn for me; treat the wounds, and do not be stunned.” He explained it as: do not be alarmed by the horror of your wounds. The eye will likewise be terrified on the Day of Resurrection.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained “when the sight is dazzled” as the moment of death, and said the dazzling of the eyes is the Hour. Mujāhid said it is at death. Qatādah said the eye is fixed and staring.

x: Regarding “and the moon is eclipsed”: its light disappears. Qatādah said the moon’s light will be gone, leaving it without light. Al-Ḥasan likewise said its light disappears.

Regarding “and the sun and moon are brought together”: God Most High says the sun and moon will be joined in the loss of their light, so neither will shine. It is reported that ʿAbd Allāh’s reading was “and the two lights are brought together.” It is also said that they will be brought together and then folded up, as in God’s words,
“When the sun is folded up”

“Brought together” is used with the meaning “joined together.” Some Kufan grammarians said it means the two lights are joined, as if the phrase were “the two illuminations were gathered.” This is al-Kisāʾī’s view.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid said the sun and moon will be folded together on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd said they will be joined and then thrown onto the earth; he cited “When the sun is folded up,” explaining that it will be folded up on the earth with the moon alongside it. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār recited this verse one day and said they will be joined on the Day of Resurrection and then thrown into the sea, becoming the great Fire of God.

evidence.text: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār recited this verse one day and said they will be joined on the Day of Resurrection and then thrown into the sea, becoming the great Fire of God.

x: Regarding “that day the human being will say, ‘Where can I flee?’”: the regional reciters read al-mafar with fatḥah on the fāʾ, because the middle root letter in the verb yafʿalu is kasrah. When the middle letter of yafʿalu has kasrah, In Arabic, the verbal noun from this verb takes fatḥah when the verb is on the yafʿilu pattern: one says farra-yafirru-mafar, meaning flight.
“O Banū Bakr, release Kulayb for me!
O Banū Bakr, where, where is escape?” When this meaning is intended, they say al-mafar with fatḥah, as they say al-madabb from dabba-yadibbu, “to creep.”
“The traces remaining along his back are like the path of ants over the sand.”

It is also recited with kasrah, though fatḥah is more common. Arabs use both; it is a verbal noun with kasrah on the middle letter. Al-Farrāʾ said both are dialects: he heard madab and madib al-sayl, “the flood’s course,” just as they say maṣaḥḥ and maṣiḥḥ in a shirt. Basrans, however, use fatḥah on the middle letter of mafʿal for a verbal noun when the verb follows yafʿilu; they allow kasrah only when mafʿal means the place one flees to, as in al-maḍrib, the place where one is struck, with kasrah on the rāʾ. It is related that Ibn ʿAbbās read the word with kasrah and said: “The mafir is the place where an animal flees.” The only reading I consider permissible is fatḥah in “al-mafar,” since the authoritative reciters agree on it and it is the recognized Arabic form when flight is meant. Here it means flight. The meaning is: when the human sees the terrors of the Resurrection, he will say, “Where can I flee from this horror that has come upon me?”

There is no escape. God, exalted is His praise, says, “No indeed! There is no refuge.” There is no flight that can benefit anyone, for fleeing will not save him, and there is no fortress, mountain, or stronghold to which he can resort from God’s command now present. Ibn ʿAbbās explained “there is no refuge” as “no shelter,” and another report says, “no fortress or place of refuge.” Muṭarrif ibn ʿAbd Allāh said “There is no refuge” means there is no mountain. When people flee, they used to say, “To the refuge!” Another report from Muṭarrif says: “No refuge—no mountain.” Al-Ḥasan said there is no mountain. He explained that in pre-Islamic times Arabs would frighten one another: two men might be with their livestock, unaware of danger, until horsemen approached; then one would say to the other, “To the refuge! To the mountain!” Al-Ḥasan, Abū Mawdūd, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Abū Qilābah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise explained it as no mountain, fortress, shelter, or escape.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said that in the language of Ḥimyar, wazar means mountain. Ibn Zayd said there is no place to hide from the matter from which there is no escape. Regarding “To your Lord that day is the final destination”: O human being, the final settlement that day is with your Lord; He assigns all His creation their places. Ibn Zayd said the people of Paradise will settle in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire. He recited,
“The true life is the life of the Hereafter, if only they knew”

Others said it means that the ultimate destination is to your Lord. Qatādah explained it as “the end point.” Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “On that day the human being will be informed of what he sent ahead and left behind. Rather, the human being will be a witness against himself, even if he offers his excuses” (75:13–15).
On that day—when the sun and moon are brought together and folded up—the human being will be told what he sent ahead and left behind.
The interpreters differed.
Some said it means the good or evil deeds he sent ahead in this world before death, and the good or evil practice he left behind after death that others act upon.

The only reading I consider permissible is fatḥah in “al-mafar,” since the authoritative reciters agree on it and it is the recognized Arabic form when flight is meant.

x: Ibn ʿAbbās said it means what a person did before death and what practice he established that was followed after his death. Ibn Masʿūd said “what he sent ahead” means his deeds, and “what he left behind” means a good or evil practice followed after him.
Others said it means the sins he sent ahead and the acts of obedience he left for later. Ibn ʿAbbās said a person will be informed of the sins he committed and the acts of obedience he delayed.
Others said it means a person’s first and last deeds. Mujāhid said his earliest and latest deeds. Other reports from Mujāhid and Ibrāhīm give the same explanation.

Others said “what he sent ahead” means obedience to God and “what he left behind” means God’s rights that he neglected. Qatādah explained it this way: the obedience he performed and the rights of God he neglected.

Others said it means whatever good or evil a person did and whatever acts of obedience he left undone. Ibn Zayd explained “what he left behind” as work he failed to do, including obedience to God he neglected, and “what he sent ahead” as the good or evil he did. In our view, the soundest interpretation is that God informs a person of everything he sent ahead—good or evil deeds performed during life—and everything he left behind after death, whether a good or evil practice he established, or a deed he was obligated to do but neglected. God did not specify one category to the exclusion of another; all of it will be disclosed to a person on the Day of Resurrection. Regarding “Rather, the human being will be a witness against himself”: God, mighty and exalted, says a person has watchers from within himself who observe his deeds and testify against him.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as his hearing, sight, hands, feet, and limbs. On this interpretation, “a witness” refers to the limbs Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned, and the phrase “against himself” is governed by them; “the human being” is understood from the pronoun in “himself.”

Others said it means the human being alone is a witness against himself. They take “a witness” as a predicate describing the human being. Ibn ʿAbbās said a person is a witness against himself alone. Qatādah said he bears witness against himself through his deeds. He remarked: You may see a person perceptive about other people’s faults and sins but heedless of his own. It was said in the Gospel: “Son of Adam, you see the speck in your brother’s eye but do not see the log lodged in your own.”
Ibn Zayd said a person is a witness against himself and recited,
“Read your book; today you are sufficient as your own reckoner”
Those who hold this view say the feminine ending in baṣīrah is used as a predicate for a person, as when one says to a man, “You are a proof against yourself.” Some Basran grammarians held this view.

Others said the feminine ending in baṣīrah is used as an adjective for a male, as in rāwiyah (“narrator”) and ʿallāmah (“great scholar”). Regarding “even if he offers his excuses”: the interpreters differed.

Some said it means that a person has witnesses from within himself, even if he excuses himself verbally for the sins and acts of disobedience he committed and argues falsely. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as making excuses. He cited,
“The excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them”
“They will offer submission to God that day”
“We did no evil”
and
“By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists”

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the person is a witness against himself even if he offers excuses. Mujāhid said the person is a witness against himself even if he argues in his own defense. ʿIkrimah was asked about the verse but remained silent. When told that al-Ḥasan says, “Son of Adam, your own deeds have the stronger claim over you,” he replied, “He spoke truly.” Ibn Zayd said these are the excuses people offer on the Day of Resurrection, but they will not benefit them. Some will not be permitted to make excuses, and others will be permitted, but their excuses will not help them; they will make false excuses.
His saying, ‘Even if he offers his excuses’: the interpreters differed about its meaning.

Some said it means that a person is a witness against himself, even if he makes verbal excuses for the sins he committed, the acts of disobedience he performed, and argues falsely. Ibn ʿAbbās explained maʿādhīr as ‘excuses,’ citing God’s words, ‘The excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them’ (Q 40:52), and ‘They will present themselves before God that Day …’ Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the human being bears witness against himself even if he makes excuses. Mujāhid said he bears witness against himself even if he argues on his own behalf. ʿIkrimah was asked about the verse and remained silent. When told that al-Ḥasan says, “Son of Adam, your own deeds have the stronger claim over you,” he replied, “He spoke truly.” Ibn Zayd said people’s excuses on the Day of Resurrection will not benefit them. Some will not be permitted to make excuses, and others will be permitted, but their excuses will not help them; they will lie.
Others said it means that a person has an inner witness against himself even if he strips himself bare. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as “even if he is naked.”
Others said it means even if he lets down the curtains and closes the doors. Al-Suddī said it means even if he draws the curtains and closes the doors.

Others said his excuses will not be accepted. Al-Ḥasan said they will not be accepted; Qatādah said even if a person offers false excuses that day, they will not be accepted on the Day of Resurrection. Another report from Qatādah says “even if he makes excuses.” In our view, the soundest interpretation is that it means “even if he makes excuses,” because this best fits the verse’s apparent meaning.

m: the human being has a witness against himself, so what naturally follows is that he may argue falsely in his own defense and make untrue excuses, but his own testimony against himself is stronger and truer than his false excuses.

x: Interpretation of the words of God Most High: “Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. It is for Us to gather it and recite it. When We recite it, follow its recitation. Then it is for Us to explain it” (75:16–19).
God Most High says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Muḥammad, do not move your tongue with the Qur’an to hasten it.
The interpreters differed over why he was told this.

Some said that when something was revealed, he would hasten to memorize it because of his love for it, so God told him not to hurry; He would preserve it for him. Ibn ʿAbbās related that when the Qur’an was revealed to the Prophet, he would hasten to memorize it, so God said, “Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. It is for Us to gather it and recite it.” Ibn ʿAbbās demonstrated by moving his lips. ʿUbayd ibn Ismāʿīl al-Habbārī and Yūnus related from Sufyān, from ʿAmr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that when the Qur’an was revealed to the Prophet, he would hasten to memorize it and move his lips. So God revealed, “Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. It is for Us to gather it and recite it.” Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the same; Sufyān moved his mouth to demonstrate. Ibn ʿAbbās said that when Gabriel came to the Prophet with revelation, the Prophet moved his tongue and lips along with it, which was difficult for him and could be seen.

Then this verse from Sūrat al-Qiyāmah was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbās also related that when the Qur’an was revealed to the Prophet, he moved his lips and this was noticeable. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr demonstrated this and explained “to hasten it” as hastening to receive it. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said Gabriel would bring the Qur’an and the Prophet would move his tongue hastily, so God told him not to do so. Al-Shaʿbī said that when revelation came, the Prophet would hurry to speak it because he loved it; then this verse was revealed. Ibn Zayd said: Do not speak what We reveal to you until its revelation is completed; when We have finished revealing it, then recite it. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the Prophet moved his tongue when a passage of the Qur’an was revealed, fearing he would forget it.

Others said the reason was that he recited the Qur’an repeatedly for fear of forgetting it. He was told: “Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. It is for Us to gather it and recite it”—We will gather it for you and teach you to recite it so you do not forget. Ibn ʿAbbās said the Prophet kept reciting without pause for fear of forgetting, so God promised to gather it for him and recite it to him. Mujāhid said the Prophet reviewed the Qur’an for fear of forgetting it; God told him, “We have taken care of it for you, Muḥammad.” Al-Ḥasan said the Prophet moved his tongue to review it, and God promised to preserve it. Qatādah said the Prophet moved his tongue for fear of forgetting, and God revealed what they heard. Another report from Qatādah says he recited the Qur’an repeatedly for fear of forgetting. In our view, the report from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr through Ibn ʿAbbās best fits the apparent meaning: “It is for Us to gather it and recite it” indicates that he was forbidden to move his tongue hastily before the revelation was gathered.

His reviewing it to remember would take place only after God had gathered what he wished to review. Regarding “It is for Us to gather it and recite it”: God Most High says: It is for Us, Muḥammad, to gather this Qur’an in your heart and establish it there. “And its recitation” means We will enable you to recite it after gathering it in your heart.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained “gather it” as gather it in your heart, and “its recitation” as reciting it afterward. Another report says God will gather it for him and teach him to recite it so he does not forget. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said God will gather it and establish it in his heart.

evidence.text: It is for Us to gather it and recite it.
When We recite it, follow its recitation.
It is for Us to gather it and recite it.”
It is for Us to gather it and recite it.”
Ibn Zayd said: Do not speak what We reveal to you until its revelation is completed; when We have finished revealing it, then recite it.
It is for Us to gather it and recite it”—We will gather it for you and teach you to recite it so you do not forget.
Ibn ʿAbbās said the Prophet kept reciting without pause for fear of forgetting, so God promised to gather it for him and recite it to him.

In our view, the report from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr through Ibn ʿAbbās best fits the apparent meaning: “It is for Us to gather it and recite it” indicates that he was forbidden to move his tongue hastily before the revelation was gathered.
Regarding “It is for Us to gather it and recite it”: God Most High says: It is for Us, Muḥammad, to gather this Qur’an in your heart and establish it there.
“And its recitation” means We will enable you to recite it after gathering it in your heart.
Another report says God will gather it for him and teach him to recite it so he does not forget.

x: Others interpreted “its recitation” as its arrangement, so the meaning is: We will gather it in your heart so you memorize it and arrange it. Qatādah said it means its preservation and arrangement. He understood Qurʾān as a verbal noun, citing the expression for a she-camel that has conceived: “the camel has gathered a fetus in her womb.” ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said: “The arms of a tall, tawny young she-camel, pure in color, that has not yet conceived a fetus.” “Has not conceived” means her womb has not gathered a young one. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk understood it as the verbal noun from qaraʾa, yaqraʾu, qurʾānan and qirāʾatan, “to recite.” Regarding “When We recite it, follow its recitation”: the interpreters differed.
Some said it means: when We reveal it to you, listen to its recitation. Ibn ʿAbbās explained “when We recite it” as “when We reveal it to you,” and “follow its recitation” as “listen to it.”

Others said that when it is recited to you, follow its laws and rulings. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as: when it is recited to you, follow what it contains. Qatādah said: Follow what it permits and avoid what it forbids. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Follow what is in it.

Others said it means: when We make it clear, act upon it. Ibn ʿAbbās explained “when We recite it” as “when We make it clear,” and “follow its recitation” as “act upon it.” In my view, the soundest interpretation is: when it is recited to you, act upon its commands and prohibitions and follow what it instructs. This is supported by God’s statement that He will gather it in the Prophet’s heart and recite it to him; as shown above, qurʾānah means “its recitation.”

evidence.text: Regarding “When We recite it, follow its recitation”: the interpreters differed.
Ibn ʿAbbās explained “when We recite it” as “when We reveal it to you,” and “follow its recitation” as “listen to it.”
Others said that when it is recited to you, follow its laws and rulings.
Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as: when it is recited to you, follow what it contains.
Ibn ʿAbbās explained “when We recite it” as “when We make it clear,” and “follow its recitation” as “act upon it.”
In my view, the soundest interpretation is: when it is recited to you, act upon its commands and prohibitions and follow what it instructs.
This is supported by God’s statement that He will gather it in the Prophet’s heart and recite it to him; as shown above, qurʾānah means “its recitation.”

x: Regarding “Then it is for Us to explain it”: God Most High says that it is for Him to explain in detail its lawful and unlawful matters and its rulings. Ibn ʿAbbās said this means explaining what is lawful and unlawful. Qatādah said it means explaining the lawful, avoiding the unlawful, and clarifying disobedience and obedience.

Others said it means that the Prophet will explain it with his tongue. Ibn ʿAbbās said “its explanation” means explaining it with your tongue. Interpretation of the words of God Most High: “No indeed! But you love the fleeting life and leave the Hereafter. Some faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord; and some faces that day will be gloomy, expecting a backbreaking calamity” (75:20–25).
God Most High says to His servants addressed by this Qur’an, who prefer the adornment of this worldly life over the Hereafter: The matter is not as you claim, people, that you do not…
On His saying, ‘Then its explanation is incumbent upon Us’: God—exalted is He—says that it is for Us to explain to you in detail what it contains of lawful and unlawful matters and rulings.
The interpreters differed. Ibn ʿAbbās said that this means its lawful and unlawful matters; Qatādah said, its lawful matters, avoidance of its prohibitions, disobedience and obedience.
Others said it means that We will make it clear through your tongue. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr transmitted this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘No indeed! Rather, you love the immediate life (20) and leave the Hereafter (21). Faces that Day will be radiant (22), looking toward their Lord (23), while faces that Day will be gloomy (24), expecting a calamity to be inflicted upon them (25).’ Abū Jaʿfar says: God addresses those spoken to by this Qur’an, who prefer the adornment of this worldly life to the Hereafter. The matter is not as you people claim—that you will not be raised after death or repaid for your deeds. What prompted you to say this is your love of the fleeting world and preference for its desires over the later life and its bliss: you believe in what is immediate and deny what is to come. Qatādah said: Most people have chosen the immediate life, except those whom God has shown mercy to and protected.

His saying, ‘Faces that Day will be radiant’: God means that on the Day of Resurrection faces will be beautiful and fair because of bliss. In Arabic one says that a person’s face has become radiant when it is made beautiful by blessing, and that God has brightened someone’s face. Some interpreters gave the same explanation. Al-Ḥasan said ‘beautiful’; Mujāhid said the faces’ radiance is their beauty. Ibn Zayd said that ‘radiant’ means enjoying blessing. Mujāhid also described them as beautiful faces, full of joy, delight, and bliss.
Others said the word means that they are joyful; Mujāhid explained it as ‘rejoicing.’
His saying, ‘looking toward their Lord’: the interpreters differed about its meaning.
Some said that the faces will look at their Lord.

Among those who said this: ʿIkrimah explained that they will truly look at their Lord. Al-Ḥasan said they will look at the Creator, and rightly be radiant while looking at Him. ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī said they will look at God, mighty and majestic, while their sight cannot encompass Him because of His greatness, whereas His sight encompasses them.

Others said instead that the faces will await reward from their Lord. Among those who held that the verse means awaiting reward: Mujāhid repeatedly explained ‘looking toward their Lord’ as waiting for reward from Him. In another report he said they await their provision and favor, or what He has ordained for them. Mujāhid was asked about people who said that God is seen; he replied that He sees, but nothing sees Him. Reports also describe the lowest-ranking inhabitant of Paradise as seeing his domain, couches, and servants across a distance of a thousand years, while the highest-ranking will look upon God’s face morning and evening. The reports continue with the same descriptions. Al-Ṭabarī says the sounder of the two interpretations is the one related from al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrimah: the faces will look at their Creator. Reports to that effect are also transmitted from the Messenger of God, blessings and peace be upon him.

ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥurr related from Muṣʿab ibn al-Miqdām, from Isrāʾīl ibn Yūnus, from Thuwayr, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Messenger of God said: ‘The lowest in rank among the people of Paradise will look over his kingdom for two thousand years, while the highest in rank will look upon God’s face twice each day.’ He then recited, ‘Faces that Day will be radiant,’ meaning bright and clear, ‘looking toward their Lord,’ that is, looking upon God’s face each day.

His saying, ‘while faces that Day will be gloomy’: God means that on that Day some faces will have changed color, darkened, and become scowling. In Arabic, one says ‘I made his face gloomy’ when one causes it to become so.
The interpreters gave similar explanations. Mujāhid explained ‘gloomy’ as scowling; Qatādah said ‘grim’; Ibn Zayd and Qatādah also said ‘frowning.’
His saying, ‘expecting a calamity to be inflicted upon them’: God says that they know a terrible disaster will befall them. A ‘fāqirah’ is a calamity.
The interpreters offered the same explanation.

Mujāhid explained it as a calamity, Qatādah as evil, and Ibn Zayd said they expect to enter the Fire—that is their calamity. The word originally refers to a mark made by breaking or branding the nose.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘No indeed! When the soul reaches the collarbones (26), and it is said, “Who can heal him?” (27), and he realizes that it is the parting (28), and one leg is entwined with the other (29), that Day he will be driven to your Lord (30).’ Abū Jaʿfar says: the matter is not as the associators imagine, that they will not be punished for their association and disobedience. Rather, when one of them is dying and his soul reaches the collarbones, he gasps. Ibn Zayd said that ‘the collarbones’ means the person himself. ‘Who can heal him?’ means that his family asks who can recite over him and cure what has afflicted him, and they seek physicians. They seek physicians and healers, but none can avert from him what God has decreed.

The interpreters differed over ‘Who can heal him?’ Some explained it as asking whether anyone can perform a healing recitation; Abū Qilābah understood it as asking for a physician who can cure, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise said it means a doctor. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk also explained it as ‘Is there anyone to treat him?’ Qatādah said they seek physicians, but they cannot avert anything of God’s decree. Ibn Zayd said it means, ‘Where are the doctors and healers—who can cure him of death?’

Others said the words are spoken by the angels to one another: ‘Who will ascend with the soul?’ Ibn ʿAbbās explained that when the soul reaches the collarbones, the angels ask which group will ascend with it: the angels of mercy or the angels of punishment. A report from Abū al-Jawzāʾ gives the same interpretation.

evidence.text: Some explained it as asking whether anyone can perform a healing recitation; Abū Qilābah understood it as asking for a physician who can cure, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise said it means a doctor.

x: His saying, ‘and he realizes that it is the parting’: the person afflicted by this knows with certainty that he is parting from the world, his family, his wealth, and his children. Qatādah said he becomes certain that it is the parting. Ibn Zayd said no one can repel or deny death, though a person may not know whether he will die from that illness or another; this is the uncertainty expressed here.
His saying, ‘and one leg is entwined with the other’: the interpreters differed.

Some said the hardship of this world has become entwined with the hardship of the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as the severity of this world joined to that of the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAbbās also said it is the last day of this world and the first day of the Hereafter, when one hardship meets another, except for those shown mercy by God. He explained that this world is joined to the Hereafter, as indicated by ‘that Day he will be driven to your Lord.’ Mujāhid said the affairs of this world become joined to those of the Hereafter at death. Other reports similarly describe the final day of this world meeting the first day of the next, and al-Ḥasan is reported to have said that the leg of this world meets the leg of the Hereafter. Ibn Mujāhid said it is the affairs of this world and the Hereafter at death. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the people of this world prepare the body while the people of the Hereafter prepare the soul; in another report, people prepare the body and the angels prepare the soul.

Other reports from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ, ʿAṭiyyah, and Mujāhid likewise interpret it as this world meeting the Hereafter. Qatādah also described it as one hardship joined to another. Ibn Zayd said scholars offered two explanations: the leg of the Hereafter joining the leg of this world, or the legs of the dead person becoming entwined. He preferred the former, citing ‘that Day he will be driven to God.’
Others said the dead person’s legs are wrapped together in his shroud. The reports continue: some said the phrase means the deceased’s legs are wrapped in the shroud.

Others said the dead person’s legs become entwined at death. ʿĀmir (al-Shaʿbī) transmitted that it means the dead man’s legs, and that they become entwined when he dies. Al-Ḥasan explained it as the legs being wrapped in the shroud.

Others said the dead person’s legs become entwined at death. Abū Mālik said it occurs at death; al-Ḥasan said God’s decree has bound the legs together; and other reports describe the person’s legs coming together. Qatādah asked whether one had not seen a person strike one leg against the other, and said that the legs die and no longer carry him anywhere, though he had once walked about on them. Al-Suddī, transmitting from Abū Mālik, also said it means the legs at death.
Others understood it as their stiffening at death.

Another group said it means one affair becoming joined to another; still others said one affliction becomes joined to another. Al-Ṭabarī considers the most sound interpretation to be that the leg of this world becomes joined to the leg of the Hereafter: the agony of death joins the terror of what is encountered beyond it. The following phrase, ‘that Day he will be driven to your Lord,’ supports this. In Arabic, any matter that becomes severe is described as having ‘bared its leg’ or ‘rolled up its sleeve.’ A poet uses the same expression. Thus ‘one leg is entwined with the other’ means that one severity is joined to another, as when a woman’s thighs are pressed together she is called laffāʾ. His saying, ‘that Day he will be driven to your Lord’: Muḥammad, that Day—the Day when one leg is entwined with the other—he will be driven to your Lord.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘He neither affirmed the truth nor prayed (31), but denied and turned away (32), then went back to his family strutting (33). Woe to you, and again woe (34)! Then woe to you, and again woe (35)! Does the human being suppose that he will be left neglected? (36)’ Abū Jaʿfar says: he did not affirm God’s Book or pray to Him; rather, he denied God’s Book and turned away from obedience to God.
The interpreters gave the same explanation.

Qatādah explained ‘he neither affirmed the truth nor prayed’ as meaning that he did not affirm God’s Book or pray to God; ‘but denied and turned away’ means that he denied God’s Book and turned away from obedience to Him. His saying, ‘then he went back to his family strutting’: God means that he returned to his family, walking arrogantly. Qatādah and Zayd ibn Aslam explained it as strutting. Zayd said it was the gait of Banū Makhzūm. Mujāhid described a Qurashī man walking in this manner and said that the person in question strutted.

Qatādah said the man was Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, whose walk was a swagger. Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd also said these verses concern Abū Jahl, strutting. ‘Yatamaṭṭā’ describes twisting or swaying his back in arrogance; al-maṭā means the back. A report from the Prophet mentions the ‘swaggering, swaying gait,’ in which a man throws his arms about and rocks from side to side. His saying, ‘Woe to you, and again woe! Then woe to you, and again woe!’ is a threat from God, mighty and majestic, following a threat. Qatādah called it one warning after another and said it was revealed concerning God’s enemy Abū Jahl.

Qatādah related that the Prophet seized Abū Jahl by the front of his garment and said, ‘Woe to you, and again woe! Then woe to you, and again woe!’ Abū Jahl replied that neither Muḥammad nor his Lord could do anything to him, and claimed he was the mightiest man between Mecca’s two mountains. Another report says that when the Prophet took Abū Jahl by the hand and recited the threat, Abū Jahl boasted of his strength; at Badr he later appeared before the Muslims, saying that God would not be worshipped after that day, and was killed. Ibn Zayd also related Abū Jahl’s boast that he was the mightiest man of Mecca and its plain. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that the Prophet first uttered the words himself, then God revealed them. The passage also cites the verses: ‘Let him call his assembly; We shall call the guards of Hell. No indeed! Do not obey him; prostrate and draw near’ (Q 96:17–19).

His saying, ‘Does the human being suppose that he will be left neglected?’ God means: does this disbelieving human suppose he will be abandoned without command or prohibition, and without being charged to worship? Ibn ʿAbbās explained sudā as ‘neglected.’ Mujāhid said it means not being commanded or forbidden. Ibn Zayd said it is one on whom no deed is imposed and who performs no deed.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Was he not a drop of emitted semen (37), then he became a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned him (38), making from him the two sexes, male and female (39)? Is not He who did that able to bring the dead to life? (40)’ Abū Jaʿfar says: God asks whether this person, who denies God’s power to restore him after death and create him after he has perished, was not a small quantity of fluid in the man’s loins, from semen that is emitted. Readers differed over ‘is emitted’: most readers of Medina and Kufa read it with a feminine tāʾ, referring to the drop being emitted; some readers of Mecca and Basra read it with a masculine yāʾ, referring to the semen being emitted. Both are established readings with sound meanings, and either is correct.

evidence.text: Readers differed over ‘is emitted’: most readers of Medina and Kufa read it with a feminine tāʾ, referring to the drop being emitted; some readers of Mecca and Basra read it with a masculine yāʾ, referring to the semen being emitted.

x: His saying, ‘then he became a clinging clot’: after being a drop of semen, he became a clot of blood. ‘And He created and proportioned him’: God formed him into a human after he had been a drop and then a clot, shaping him as a complete person who speaks, hears, and sees. ‘Making from him the two sexes, male and female’: from this person, after making him sound in form, God produced offspring, male and female. ‘Is not He who did that able to bring the dead to life?’ The One who made a human from a drop, then a clot, until he became a fully formed person with sons and daughters, is surely able to revive the dead after their death and restore them as they were. The One capable of this creation cannot be thwarted in bringing a dead person back to life. When the Messenger of God recited this verse, he would say, ‘Yes indeed.’ Qatādah related that it had been told to them that when the Prophet recited it, he said, ‘Glory be to You, and yes indeed.’ This is the end of the commentary on Sūrat al-Qiyāmah.

evidence.text: When the Messenger of God recited this verse, he would say, ‘Yes indeed.’
Qatādah related that it had been told to them that when the Prophet recited it, he said, ‘Glory be to You, and yes indeed.’

notes.en: Reading note: قرأ المدنيان بفتح الراء وهى أيضًا قراءة زيد بن ثابت ونصر بن عاصم وعبد الله بن أبي إسحاق وأبى حيوة وابن أبي عبلة والزعفرانى وابن مقسم وزيد بن علي وأبان from عاصم وهارون ومحبوب كلاهما from أبي عمرو والحسن والجحدرى بخلاف عنهما بفتحها. وقرأ Ibn Kathir وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائى ويعقوب وخلف، كلهم بكسرها. see النشر 2/ 294، وتفسير البحر المحيط 8/ 385.

notes.en: Al-Suyuti cites the report in al-Durr al-Manthur 6/295 to the author. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: ‘If it is said that Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Mansur, from Mujahid, regarding God’s words “Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord,” that they are beautiful and await the reward, the answer is that we have not claimed consensus on this question; if there were consensus, we would have no need to argue it. Mujahid’s view is rejected because of the established Sunnah from the Prophet, the statements of the Companions, and the majority of the early authorities. Although Mujahid was among the foremost in knowledge of Qur’anic interpretation, he held two interpretations that the scholars set aside and rejected: this one, and his interpretation of God’s words “Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praised station” (Q 17:79) …’ See al-Tamhid 7/157–158.
